source.title: A U-turn on Double Descent: Rethinking Parameter Counting in Statistical Learning
source.authors: Alicia Curth; Alan Jeffares; M. van der Schaar

record.tranche_reason: The study reproduces and reanalyzes non-deep double-descent experiments, arguing that the apparent curves arise from switching between distinct ways of increasing parameters and that effective test-time parameter counts reveal ordinary convex curves.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own test-error experiments and effective-parameter measurements. Many values appear only in figures, so they are recorded as figure only; the text also explicitly describes the qualitative shapes. Results cited from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study replicates Belkin et al.'s non-deep double-descent sweeps (trees, boosting, RFF regression) on MNIST. It decomposes each composite axis into two mechanisms, each of which gives a U- or L-shaped curve. It moves the peak by changing the switch point. Plotting test error against a test-time effective parameter count gives convex curves. These results argue V4 is an artifact of parameter counting (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that non-deep double descent in trees, boosting and RFF regression arises from switching between two complexity axes, each of which is convex. Peak location is not inherently tied to interpolation, and test-time effective parameter counts fold the curves back into U-shapes. Whether this applies to deep learning is left open.
record.recipe_differences: The study says it closely follows and reproduces the non-neural experiments of Belkin et al. (2019), then adds separate-axis sweeps, altered transition points, and generalized effective-parameter measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The apparent peak location and presence depend on when the sequence switches between parameter-increasing mechanisms. Increasing ensemble size or excess features also changes the effective-parameter/test-error contours.

fits_no_version.finding: Generalization curves with arbitrarily many peaks, including peaks at P>n, are created by alternating between P_PC and P_ex increases. Training error decreases monotonically throughout.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multiple descent can be produced purely by reordering the mechanisms that add parameters, independent of noise or interpolation.

fits_no_version.finding: In fixed-design (in-sample) prediction, all interpolating models have identical expected error, so a second descent is impossible (Proposition 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A second descent cannot occur for in-sample prediction error in the interpolation regime.

record.peer_reviewed: 37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2023)
record.problems: The reported curves are primarily figures without numerical tables, uncertainty estimates, or statistical tests. Effective-parameter results for the full experiment are described as plotting the 10 one-vs-all models individually; the text does not provide numerical aggregate estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No material claim-bearing results left out. Appendix binary test-error plots (Figures 14–16) are described as qualitatively identical to the main squared-loss plots and were not separately extracted.

untested.parts: Deep-network model-size double descent; explicitly left to future work.
Epoch and sample-size axes; deep networks.
Label-noise dependence and the effect of optimal regularization. Multiple peaks are produced, but by switching mechanisms, not by noise.
Deep networks; effective-parameter definitions other than p_test.

missing.what: Multiple-descent curves from repeated mechanism switching in RFF regression
Training-error trajectories showing the second descent occurs without reaching zero training error
missing.locator: Appendix E.2 Fig 12; Appendix E.4 Figs 17–19

missing.what: p_train and p_test do not increase past the transition threshold on the composite axis
Replications on SVHN and CIFAR-10 showing the same decompositions and the Back-to-U fold
Theoretical impossibility of a second descent in fixed-design in-sample error

record.verdict_notes: Results are figure-only, with no uncertainty estimates or statistical tests. R1–R3 are the authors' replications of an original source (BHMM19), so the V4 support label rests on reproduction, not independent new evidence. R10–R12 were moved from V5 to V4/V7 because p_test removes the peak rather than predicting where it falls. Binary-loss plots (Figs 14–16) are described as qualitatively identical to the squared-loss plots.

versions.untested_parts: Changing training sample size near an interpolation threshold.
Deep networks and model classes beyond the tested trees, gradient boosting, and random Fourier feature linear regression.
The epochs and sample-size axes; the study examines parameter-increasing mechanisms in non-deep methods.
Label-noise dependence, regularization, and noise- or regularization-driven multiple peaks.
Deep networks and effective-parameter definitions other than the study's proposed generalized test-time measure.

tranche.reason: The study reproduces non-neural double descent and explicitly argues that its interpretation requires restating because complexity mechanisms and parameter counting determine the apparent shape.

source_check.notes: Figure 9 uses the 0-vs-all subproblem; the earlier main sweeps sum squared loss across ten classes. Separate results missing from these rows include multiple peaks from repeated switches (Figures 6(b), 13) and SVHN/CIFAR-10 replications (Appendix E.6).

statements.correction: Mechanism-switch changes move or remove peaks; second descent can occur without attaining zero training error; no single effective-complexity predictor of peak location is evaluated.
statements.problem: The reported switch and interpolation findings are correct, but the V5 scope-limit attribution equates an interpolation threshold with the unspecified single effective-complexity predictor in V5.
